strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: efficient deployment of DiT-based Real-ISR models via post-training quantization. It is, to my knowledge, the first systematic PTQ study tailored to DiT-based Real-ISR, and it targets aggressive W4A6/W4A4 settings.

The proposed framework is practical: H-SVD and VaSMP require no calibration data, and VaTMP uses only a small calibration set. This is a meaningful advantage over many PTQ methods that require large calibration sets or iterative optimization.

The method combines several sensible ideas: hierarchical SVD for weight reconstruction, variance-aware cross-layer weight bit allocation, and variance-aware temporal activation bit allocation via dynamic programming.

The experimental evaluation is broad: four real-world SR benchmarks, two quantization settings, multiple full-reference and no-reference metrics, and comparisons against many recent quantization and PEFT baselines.
Ablation studies and visual comparisons suggest that H-SVD, VaSMP, and VaTMP each contribute to preserving textures and local details under aggressive quantization.
weaknesses: The central H-SVD claim is not convincingly isolated. The paper compares H-SVD against a baseline without H-SVD and against SVD-G only in a non-quantized layer visualization (Fig. 4), but it does not provide an end-to-end comparison to a global SVD branch with the same total parameter and FLOP budget. Since H-SVD adds an extra FP local branch on top of SVD-G, the observed gains could come simply from additional parameters/computation rather than from the hierarchical decomposition itself.

VaSMP and VaTMP are not compared against existing mixed-precision or temporal quantization methods such as HAWQ, MixDQ, Temporal Dynamic Quantization, or MPQ-DM. VaSMP is only compared to a naive global-MSE mixed-precision baseline, and VaTMP is only compared to disabling temporal scheduling. This leaves the specific advantage of the proposed variance-aware designs unclear.

The SOTA claim is overstated. In Table 1(a), SVDQuant and QuaRot obtain better LPIPS than Q-DiT4SR on DrealSR/RealSR, and EfficientDM often obtains higher MANIQA. In Table 1(b), SVDQuant obtains better LPIPS on DrealSR/RealSR, and several baselines obtain higher MANIQA. The paper acknowledges metric mismatch for MANIQA but still claims SOTA across settings.

There is a technical inconsistency in VaSMP. The distortion model is derived for quantizing the Hadamard-transformed weight W_H, but when H-SVD is enabled the quantized tensor is the residual W_res - W_SVD-L. It is unclear whether the variance statistics are recomputed on this residual. If the original W_H variance is used, the bit allocation may be mismatched to the actual tensor being quantized.

Reproducibility is limited. No code or URL is provided, and important implementation details are missing: the DP segment count and state definition, block-size search procedure for SVD-L, how baselines were adapted to DiT4SR, number of diffusion timesteps, random seeds, and hyperparameters. The claimed 5.8x size and 6.14x operation reductions are not accompanied by wall-clock latency or memory measurements, and per-timestep/per-layer mixed bit-widths may not yield practical speedups on current hardware.

The evaluation is incomplete for a super-resolution paper: LPIPS is reported only for two datasets, and there are no FID/KID/PSNR/SSIM results. No inference latency, throughput, energy, or hardware deployment analysis is provided. There is also no dedicated limitations section.

Baseline fairness is unclear. Some baselines are QAT/PEFT methods (EfficientDM, QueST) or were designed for LLM or text-to-image DiT quantization, not DiT-based Real-ISR. Calibration budgets differ across methods, and the paper does not discuss parity of tuning or calibration data.

The local rank-1 block-wise SVD branch is somewhat heuristic. The paper does not analyze how block sizes are chosen per layer, why rank-1 per block is preferable to rank-k per block, or how the local branch interacts with quantization granularity and clipping.

strengths: Addresses a timely and practically relevant problem: efficient low-bit deployment of DiT-based Real-ISR models, which is under-explored relative to U-Net/LLM quantization.

The overall framework is coherent and modular, combining weight reconstruction (H-SVD), cross-layer weight mixed precision (VaSMP), and timestep-wise activation mixed precision (VaTMP), with a spatio-temporal grid tying them together.

VaSMP's fully data-free allocation and VaTMP's small calibration footprint are practically attractive, and the rate-distortion/water-filling derivation (Eqs. 12–16) and DP-based temporal scheduling (Eqs. 20–23) are technically reasonable.
The empirical study is broad: four real-world benchmarks, two bit settings (W4A6, W4A4), many baselines, plus ablations on SVD-L rank, VaSMP, and VaTMP, and a visualized scheduling pattern (Fig. 9).
The paper candidly notes that no-reference IQA metrics can be misleading for heavily quantized diffusion models, which is a useful observation for the community.
weaknesses: The central SOTA claim is contradicted by the paper's own full-reference results: on LPIPS, SVDQuant beats Q-DiT4SR in both reported W4A6 datasets (DrealSR 0.3829 vs 0.3880; RealSR 0.3371 vs 0.3386) and in W4A4, at the SAME parameter/operation budget (Fig. 1 shows both at 465M/2776G). The statement that Q-DiT4SR 'consistently outperforms prior approaches' is therefore not supported by the reported evidence.

Selective metric reporting: LPIPS is shown only for DrealSR and RealSR, and is omitted for RealLR200 and RealLQ250. Since LPIPS is the only full-reference metric and the method loses it where reported, the omission is a serious concern for the strength of the SOTA claim.

On MANIQA under W4A4 (DrealSR), Q-DiT4SR (0.4030) ranks below FP (0.4483) and below Q-Diffusion, EfficientDM, PTQ4DiT, PassionSR, and FlatQuant, so the 'best overall performance' claim is not robust across reported metrics; the paper relies on metrics it simultaneously argues are unreliable.
Overstated qualitative claims: the assertion of 'only marginal perceptual differences compared to the FP model' under W4A4 is inconsistent with LPIPS degrading from 0.3897 to 0.4327.

Incremental technical novelty: H-SVD essentially augments SVDQuant's global low-rank branch with a block-wise rank-1 residual under a matched budget; VaSMP is a standard variance-driven water-filling allocation with a closed-form solution; VaTMP is a segment-constrained DP. Each is a sensible but modest extension rather than a new principle.

Baseline fairness is questionable: comparisons include LLM-oriented quantization (QuaRot, FlatQuant) and PEFT methods (QueST, EfficientDM) whose results are anomalously poor (e.g., QueST MUSIQ ~40, LIQE ~1.0), raising the possibility of under-tuned or misapplied baselines that inflate the apparent margin.

Reproducibility gaps: code/models are only promised ('will be available'), and key hyperparameters (bit-width search range B, DP segment constraints, discretization details) are underspecified; results are single runs with no error bars or variance.

Despite the efficiency motivation, no wall-clock latency, memory, or throughput measurements are provided; only parameter counts and Ops are reported, which do not capture the cost of the added FP low-rank branches.
Presentation issues: the abstract is truncated ('will be available at' with no link), and there are formatting/spacing inconsistencies (e.g., 'spatio-temporal') that reduce polish.

strengths: The paper targets a genuine gap: it is (to my knowledge) the first PTQ framework designed specifically for DiT-based Real-ISR, whereas prior SR quantization work targets U-Net or one-step SR models and generic DiT quantization targets text-to-image. This is a useful and timely direction.

H-SVD is a clean, well-motivated design: combining a global low-rank branch (SVD-G) with a local block-wise rank-1 branch (SVD-L) under a matched parameter budget is sensible, and the PCA/frequency analyses in Figs. 4 and 2 provide intuitive support for why residual/local information matters for texture reconstruction.

VaSMP is derived from a defensible rate-distortion argument (high-rate quantization error scaling with per-layer weight variance), and the resulting log-variance bit-allocation rule (Eq. 16) with greedy discretization is simple and calibration-free.

VaTMP formulates timestep-wise activation precision allocation as a segmented DP problem with a normalized distortion coefficient kappa(b), which is principled and requires only a tiny LR calibration set (32 crops).

The experimental section is broad: four real-world benchmarks (DrealSR, RealSR, RealLR200, RealLQ250), ten comparison methods spanning PTQ, DiT-specific, diffusion, SR-specific, and PEFT approaches, plus ablations and visual results.

The reported efficiency gains are practically meaningful (about 5.8x smaller and 6.14x fewer operations under W4A4), and the W4A6/W4A4 split with the corresponding ablation (Tables 3-4) is a reasonable way to isolate the contribution of each component.
weaknesses: The central SOTA claim is not fully supported. On the only full-reference metric (LPIPS), SVDQuant consistently outperforms Q-DiT4SR in both W4A6 (e.g., DrealSR 0.3829 vs 0.3880; RealSR 0.3371 vs 0.3386) and W4A4 (DrealSR 0.3821 vs 0.4327; RealSR 0.3268 vs 0.3665). The paper claims best 'overall' performance but never directly addresses that it loses on the one metric that is not a no-reference IQA score.

The evaluation leans heavily on no-reference IQA metrics (MUSIQ, MANIQA, CLIPIQA, LIQE), which the authors themselves concede can be mismatched with perceptual quality ('visibly noisy reconstructions may still obtain relatively high scores ... such as MANIQA'). Since the paper's entire premise is detail preservation, the reliance on metrics the authors distrust is a serious evidential weakness, and SVDQuant even exceeding FP on LPIPS raises further questions about the reliability of the comparison.

Ablation gains are modest and sometimes non-monotonic. VaSMP improves MUSIQ only from 67.46 to 67.72 over H-SVD (Table 3) and VaSMP actually lowers LIQE (3.091 vs 3.191 in Table 4); the naive MP baseline degrades some metrics, making it a weak point of comparison. The SVD-L rank study (Table 2) is contradictory: MUSIQ monotonically increases with rank (66.71 to 68.01), yet rank 8 is chosen, and the claim that higher ranks bring 'marginal or even negative improvements' holds only for some metrics.

No wall-clock or hardware latency measurements are provided. Per-timestep, per-layer mixed-precision bit assignments create irregular kernels that frequently do not translate into real speedups; the 5.8x/6.14x figures are theoretical size/FLOP counts and are essentially identical to SVDQuant's (465/2,776), so the efficiency advantage is not unique to this method.

Reproducibility is only partially addressed: the DP formulation for the piecewise-constant temporal schedule, the exact handling of the 'matched budget' search (Eqs. 7-9), and the details of the naive MP baseline are not fully specified, and code is only promised. The reference list contains duplicated/incorrect entries (e.g., multiple 'Wang et al. 2024' for different papers, mismatched Liu entries), which hinders follow-up.

There is no dedicated limitations section; while the paper briefly notes metric mismatch, it does not discuss failure modes of the Gaussian/high-rate assumptions underlying VaSMP/VaTMP or the conditions under which the approach may break down.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: efficient deployment of DiT-based Real-ISR via post-training quantization, with a framework tailored to this setting.

H-SVD is a sensible hierarchical weight decomposition that combines a global low-rank branch with a local block-wise rank-1 branch, motivated by PCA/frequency analysis and designed under a parameter-budget constraint.

VaSMP provides a calibration-free, variance-aware cross-layer weight bit allocation, while VaTMP schedules activation precision across diffusion timesteps via dynamic programming, reducing calibration overhead relative to many prior methods.

The empirical study is broad: four real-world SR benchmarks, W4A6 and W4A4 settings, numerous quantization baselines, ablations for H-SVD/VaSMP/VaTMP, runtime/memory profiling, backbone generalization, calibration robustness, and artifact analysis.
The paper includes a candid limitations discussion and reports practical memory and end-to-end speedup measurements rather than only theoretical operation reductions.
weaknesses: The central claim of SOTA under both W4A6 and W4A4 is not fully supported by the presented results. Under W4A4, Q-DiT4SR is consistently worse than Q-Diffusion, EfficientDM, and PTQ4DiT on MANIQA, and worse than SVDQuant on LPIPS; under W4A6, SVDQuant also has better LPIPS. The paper acknowledges MANIQA mismatch but still overclaims SOTA without qualification.

The evaluation lacks standard full-reference fidelity metrics such as PSNR/SSIM for most datasets and relies heavily on no-reference IQA metrics, which the paper itself notes can be unreliable for heavily quantized generative SR. This weakens the evidence for the claimed detail preservation.

Reproducibility details are insufficient: the DP formulation for VaTMP does not specify the number of segments, regularization/segment penalty, or how the piecewise-constant constraint is enforced; hyperparameters such as b_min, b_max, B_target, and the discretization handling when the floor sum exceeds the budget are missing; calibration details and baseline calibration budgets are not reported.

The theoretical model for VaSMP ignores that H-SVD changes the residual weight distribution. Bit allocation is based on the variance of the original Hadamard-domain weights rather than the residual after subtracting the low-rank branches, so the distortion model may not match the actual quantized layer.

Novelty is incremental: H-SVD combines existing ingredients (Hadamard transform, truncated SVD, block-wise rank-1 approximation), VaSMP resembles standard reverse water-filling from variance, and VaTMP is closely related to temporal dynamic quantization. The 'first' claim is plausible but limited to DiT-based Real-ISR.

Generalization evidence is limited: DreamClear is evaluated only against the FP model, not against other quantization baselines, and W4A4 on DreamClear degrades substantially relative to FP, making it difficult to assess robustness.

Comparison fairness is unclear: several baselines are designed for U-Net diffusion or generic DiT text-to-image models and may not be optimally adapted to DiT-based Real-ISR, while calibration data and tuning budgets for baselines are not specified. Results appear to be from single runs without variance or confidence intervals.

Some internal inconsistencies remain: e.g., DrealSR W4A6 LPIPS is better than FP while RealSR is worse; the claimed 'matched parameter budget' in H-SVD is not clearly reflected in the final setting where SVD-G rank 32 is used but SVD-L rank 8 is selected; reported 5.8x model-size reduction contrasts with about 3.8x peak-memory reduction.

strengths: Addresses a practically important problem: accelerating DiT-based real-world image super-resolution via post-training quantization, which is a relevant and under-explored deployment setting.

The overall pipeline is coherent and reasonably motivated: H-SVD targets weight approximation, VaSMP handles cross-layer weight precision, and VaTMP handles timestep-dependent activation precision, which is a sensible decomposition of the error sources.
The data-free weight allocation (VaSMP) and the very small calibration set for VaTMP are appealing and align with the practical goal of lightweight PTQ.

The experimental effort is fairly broad: four real-world benchmarks, W4A6/W4A4 settings, ablations of each component, backbone generalization to DreamClear, calibration-domain robustness, and an artifact/limitations analysis (Sec. 4.6) that is refreshingly candid.
weaknesses: The central SOTA claim is not well supported. On the full-reference perceptual metric LPIPS, SVDQuant actually outperforms Q-DiT4SR under both W4A6 (e.g., DrealSR 0.3829 vs 0.3880; RealSR 0.3371 vs 0.3386) and W4A4 (DrealSR 0.3821 vs 0.4327; RealSR 0.3268 vs 0.3665). Since LPIPS is the most direct measure of the 'detail-preserving' property the paper claims as its main contribution, this directly undercuts the thesis, yet it is not discussed.

The claimed advantage rests almost entirely on no-reference IQA metrics (MUSIQ, MANIQA, CLIPIQA, LIQE) which the paper itself admits are unreliable for quantized generative restoration ('mismatch between perceptual quality and metric responses'). Using metrics the authors concede are not trustworthy as the primary evidence for SOTA is a serious evidential gap.

Limited technical novelty. H-SVD is essentially SVDQuant's low-rank-plus-residual scheme augmented with a Monarch-like block rank-1 branch; VaSMP is a standard reverse-waterfilling/rate-distortion bit allocation (Eqs. 12-16 are textbook); VaTMP is a DP temporal scheduler closely related to Temporal Dynamic Quantization (So et al., 2023). The contribution is largely a recombination of existing ideas, and the 'first' claim is only weakly justified given PassionSR already targets diffusion-based SR.

The efficiency benefit is overstated. Table 5 shows Q-DiT4SR uses more peak memory than SVDQuant (3974.64 vs 3722.83 MiB) and slightly less end-to-end speedup (4.5x vs 4.8x), so it is not more efficient than the compared method it positions itself against.

Internal inconsistency / unclear formulation: the paper repeatedly claims a 'matched parameter budget' for SVD-L, yet Table 2 shows parameter count varying from 454.78M to 529.06M with the 'rank budget' of SVD-L, and it is never clarified what 'rank' means for an always-rank-1 block decomposition. The budget-matching argument (Eqs. 7-9) therefore appears inconsistent with the reported results.

Reproducibility is incomplete. Code/models are not yet available; the H-SVD branch's claimed ~3% overhead and the Triton kernel implementation (invoking Monarch-like structured computation) are asserted but not verifiable from the manuscript, and no kernel-level validation is provided.

Presentation problems: the abstract ends with a dangling sentence ('Our code and models will be available at'); parameter/ops reporting in Fig. 1 vs the text is confusing; and the unexplained pattern of a quantized model matching or exceeding the FP model on several metrics is only hand-waved as a 'mild perceptual regularizer'.

strengths: The paper targets a practical and underexplored problem: PTQ for DiT-based Real-ISR, where existing quantization work focuses on U-Net or text-to-image DiTs. The motivation and deployment bottleneck are clearly stated.

H-SVD is a sensible hierarchical weight reconstruction scheme combining a global low-rank branch with local block-wise rank-1 branches, and Fig. 4 provides PCA evidence that the local branch better aligns with the FP model.

VaSMP and VaTMP are technically reasonable: VaSMP derives a data-free weight bit allocation from rate-distortion theory, and VaTMP uses dynamic programming over timestep-wise activation variance. Ablations in Tables 3 and 4 show consistent gains over the baseline and a naive mixed-precision baseline.

The empirical study is broad: four real-world SR benchmarks, ten comparison methods, W4A6 and W4A4 settings, ablation studies, runtime/memory profiling, generalization to DreamClear, calibration robustness, and artifact analysis.

The paper is transparent about limitations, including the lack of native arbitrary-precision kernels, residual W4A4 artifacts, and the mismatch between no-reference IQA metrics and perceptual quality.
Reproducibility is reasonably supported by detailed calibration settings (32 LR images from RealSR, 128x128 crops), the DP formulation, and a promise to release code/models.
weaknesses: The central W4A4 SOTA claim is weakened by full-reference results: SVDQuant achieves better LPIPS on all four datasets (e.g., DrealSR 0.3821 vs. 0.4327; RealSR 0.3268 vs. 0.3665), while Q-DiT4SR wins mainly on no-reference IQA metrics that the paper itself notes can be unreliable (e.g., DreamClear W4A6 exceeding FP). PSNR/SSIM are not reported.

The H-SVD parameter budget is not clearly matched to the baselines. Sec. 3.2.3-3.2.4 indicate SVD-G uses rank r and SVD-L is matched to P_SVD-G(r), so the total FP branch budget may exceed a single rank-r SVD branch. Table 2 shows monotonic parameter increases with rank, and the selected rank 8 gives 465.39M parameters, matching SVDQuant in Fig. 1 despite adding a local branch. The ablation confounds rank budget with parameter count, so it is unclear whether H-SVD's gains come from hierarchy or simply extra parameters.

VaSMP is derived only from weight variance and ignores activation magnitudes and downstream sensitivity; the comparison is limited to a naive global-MSE mixed-precision baseline rather than established calibration-based mixed-precision methods (e.g., HAWQ, MixDQ) or uniform-bit controls with matched average bits.

The practical efficiency claims are partially undermined because VaSMP/VaTMP assign non-uniform bit-widths but are mapped to standard low-bit linear computations (Sec. 4.6); native arbitrary-precision kernels are not used, so the accuracy gains may not translate to real hardware speedups. Table 6 also shows theoretical 6.14x op reduction but measured 4.51x end-to-end speedup.

The 'first PTQ framework for DiT-based Real-ISR' claim needs clearer differentiation from prior SR-specific quantization work such as PassionSR and Bimacosr, and the main evaluation uses only one backbone (DiT4SR) with a limited DreamClear check.

Several baselines (e.g., Q-Diffusion, EfficientDM, PTQ4DiT, QueST) are designed for different architectures or settings and are applied off-the-shelf; tuning details are absent, which may overstate the advantage under W4A4.
The paper lacks full-reference PSNR/SSIM for restoration benchmarks, making it harder to assess fidelity beyond LPIPS and no-reference IQA metrics.
